periods.activity_title: Counting in Groups — Arrays, Stacks and Trays

tasks_in_class.description: Count the coconut trees in Gundappa's land from the top-view grid. Write the number. How do you know?
Gundappa plucked 5 coconuts from each tree. How many coconuts has he plucked?
How many coconut laddoos are there in the trays?
How many milk pedas are there in the trays?

time_bands.activity: Open with the textbook picture of Gundappa's coconut-tree grid. Children study the top-view array and work on Let Us Count, p.34 ("Count the coconut trees in Gundappa's land...."). Each child writes their count and briefly shares with a partner how they grouped the trees — by row, by column, or some other way.

Children tackle Let Us Count, p.34 ("Gundappa plucked 5 coconuts from each tree...."), using the count they just found to compute the total harvest. Invite two or three children to explain their working aloud — skip-counting, repeated addition, or any grouping strategy they chose.

Move to the tray pictures. Children work on Let Us Count, p.34 ("How many coconut laddoos are there in the trays?") and Let Us Count, p.34 ("How many milk pedas are there in the trays?"). Encourage them to draw rings around equal groups on the page before writing the count.

Brief share-out: ask two or three children to show their grouping on the board picture. Discuss how grouping into equal sets makes counting quicker than counting one by one. Additional practice: Let Us Count Q3 (cups), p.34 may be used as extension for children who finish early.

periods.teacher_notes: Children at this stage often count pictorial arrays one-by-one rather than in rows or columns; prompt them to draw loops around equal groups before counting. Watch for children who recount from one when switching from laddoos to pedas — the grouping strategy transfers directly. T-3 (cups) is a structurally identical array task; it is noted as additional practice rather than a separate in-class item.
materials: Pencils and crayons for circling groups

periods.activity_title: Arranging and Reading Money — Same Amount, Different Arrangements

tasks_in_class.description: Look at Shirley's coin arrangement (circular pattern). How much money is it?
How did you count them? Discuss in class.
Arrange play money of amounts 1, 2, 5, and 10 to show ₹36, ₹125, and ₹183. Ask your peers to tell how much it is.
Shirley and Shiv arranged coins in groups. Write the number of coins in the blank triangles for each arrangement.

time_bands.activity: Distribute play-money sets (₹1, ₹2, ₹5, ₹10 coins and notes). Children open to p.35 and study Shirley's circular coin arrangement, then work on Patterns with Money, p.35 ("Look at Shirley's coin arrangement (circular pattern). How much money is it?"). Each child writes the total.

Class discussion on Patterns with Money, p.35 ("How did you count them?"). Collect three or four different strategies — grouping by denomination, skip-counting in fives, adding largest coins first. Record the strategies briefly on the board so children can see multiple valid routes to the same answer.

Pairs use their play-money sets for Patterns with Money, p.35 ("Arrange play money...to show ₹36, ₹125, and ₹183...."). One partner arranges, the other reads the total aloud. Swap roles for each amount. Roam to listen for denomination choices.

Children complete Two Ways, p.35 ("Shirley and Shiv arranged coins in groups. Write the number of coins in the blank triangles...."), noticing that Shirley groups in 3s and 5s while Shiv groups in 4s. Close by asking: does the arrangement change how many coins there are? T-7 (Shiv's notes-and-coins grid) is structurally similar to T-6 and is noted as additional practice.

periods.teacher_notes: A common error is adding coin face values without attending to denomination — for example, counting three ₹5 coins as 3 rather than 15. Draw attention to the denomination printed on each coin before children begin. The 'Two Ways' activity introduces the idea that the same quantity can be structured into different equal groups, which underpins the even-odd pairing explored in the units that follow.

periods.activity_title: Pairing Coins — Discovering Even and Odd

tasks_in_class.book_ref: Two Ways / Even and Odd, p.36
tasks_in_class.description: Describe Shiv's arrangement and write his numbers.

tasks_in_class.book_ref: Two Ways / Even and Odd, p.36
tasks_in_class.description: Describe Shirley's arrangement and write her numbers.
Identify numbers between 1 and 20 as even or odd. You may draw the pairing arrangement.
Do you think all numbers in the times-2 table are even?

time_bands.activity: Children use actual coins (or counters) to re-enact Shiv and Shirley's coin arrangements from p.36. They physically pair the coins in twos — first Shiv's collection, then Shirley's — and notice which collection pairs perfectly and which has one left over.

Children work on Two Ways / Even and Odd, p.36 ("Describe Shiv's arrangement and write his numbers") and Two Ways / Even and Odd, p.36 ("Describe Shirley's arrangement and write her numbers"). They write what they observe — 'pairs with none left over' vs 'one always left over' — in their own words before attaching the labels even and odd.
Children complete Even and Odd, p.36 ("Identify numbers between 1 and 20 as even or odd...."), drawing pairing diagrams for any number they are unsure about. Pairs check each other's lists.

Open inquiry: Even and Odd, p.36 ("Do you think all numbers in the times-2 table are even?"). Children list the first ten multiples of 2, pair each one with counters or a quick diagram, and share their conclusion with the class.

periods.teacher_notes: Children sometimes call a number 'odd' simply because it looks unfamiliar rather than applying the pairing test; insist that they physically or pictorially pair before labelling. The pairing-of-coins model built here — even numbers pair completely, odd numbers leave one over — is the concrete anchor for the chart-based and digit-based reasoning that follows in the crayons arrangement unit.
materials: Coins or counters (at least 20 per child)

periods.activity_title: The Crayons Chart — Classifying and Noticing Patterns

tasks_in_class.description: Circle the odd numbers and put a square around each even number from the given set (5, 8, 36, 69, 22, 51, 30, 38, 37, 52, 43). Use the crayons arrangement if needed.
Explore your textbook and find out what Shirley has seen. Draw a square on the even page numbers. Put a circle on the odd page numbers.
Shirley notices numbers before and after an odd number are even. Shiv wonders if numbers before and after an even number are odd. Check and discuss.

time_bands.activity: Children open to the crayons chart on p.37, which shows 1–50 with odd and even numbers in adjacent columns. They study the visual layout, then complete Crayons Arrangement, p.37 ("Circle the odd numbers and put a square around each even number from the given set...."), using the chart as a reference tool. Circulate and note who still needs to count pairs and who reads the column directly.

Children explore their textbook page numbers for Crayons Arrangement, p.37 ("Explore your textbook and find out what Shirley has seen. Draw a square on the even page numbers. Put a circle on the odd page numbers."). They flip through several pages, mark a sample, and discuss what pattern they see in the sequence of page numbers.

Children investigate Even and Odd, p.38 ("Shirley notices numbers before and after an odd number are even. Shiv wonders if numbers before and after an even number are odd. Check and discuss."). They test three or four examples each — choosing their own numbers — before sharing their findings. Consolidate with a quick class vote: is the pattern always true?

periods.teacher_notes: Children sometimes classify two-digit numbers by the tens digit rather than the units digit; the crayons chart makes the units-digit pattern visible — point out the column headings explicitly. The page-number exploration is particularly motivating because children discover the pattern in a familiar object; let them announce their discovery before you confirm it.

periods.activity_title: Consecutive Numbers, Digit Rules and Making Even Numbers

tasks_in_class.description: Choose any 10 consecutive numbers. Write whether they are even or odd below each number. What do you notice? Discuss.
Identify which of the following numbers are even and which are odd. Explain your reasoning: 30, 78, 300, 415, 46, 67, 154, 99.
Make two 2-digit numbers using digits 1 and 6 without repetition; identify as even or odd. Then choose any two digits and make 2-digit even numbers.

homework.description: Are there more even or odd numbers between 1 and 100?

time_bands.activity: Each child chooses their own starting number and writes ten consecutive numbers. They label each E (even) or O (odd) beneath it, then look for the pattern in the sequence. Small groups of three compare starting numbers — did everyone get the same alternating pattern regardless of where they started?

Children work on Even and Odd, p.38 ("Identify which of the following numbers are even and which are odd. Explain your reasoning: 30, 78, 300, 415, 46, 67, 154, 99."). The emphasis is on the explanation: they must write or say which digit they looked at and why, not just produce a label.

Children tackle Even and Odd, p.38 ("Make two 2-digit numbers using digits 1 and 6 without repetition; identify as even or odd. Then choose any two digits and make 2-digit even numbers."). Invite children to share the digit pairs they chose and how they arranged the digits to guarantee an even result.

periods.teacher_notes: The key generalisation in this unit is that the units digit alone determines even or odd for any whole number; children may still be distracted by large numbers and check every digit. Prompt them: 'Which digit tells you?' whenever they hesitate on a three-digit number. T-21 is set as homework because it is a counting-and-reasoning task that extends the in-class pattern work without requiring any new materials.
materials: Squared or plain paper for consecutive-number rows

periods.activity_title: Reasoning About Even and Odd — A Whole-Chapter Game

tasks_in_class.description: Are there more even or odd numbers between 1 and 100?

time_bands.activity: Pose the question from Even and Odd, p.38 ("Are there more even or odd numbers between 1 and 100?") as an open investigation. Children make a written prediction first and give a brief reason. Record predictions on the board — more even, more odd, or equal — without revealing the answer.

Children work in pairs: one lists all even numbers 1–100, the other lists all odd numbers, counting as they go. They then compare totals and use the crayons chart (p.37) and the consecutive-number pattern to explain why the counts come out as they do.

Class discussion: pairs report their counts and reasoning. Guide the class to articulate the alternating pattern — for every even number there is exactly one odd neighbour — and connect it to the earlier pairing model. Children write a sentence in their own words: 'Between 1 and 100 there are ___ even numbers and ___ odd numbers because ___.'.
Quick oral round: teacher calls a number (up to three digits), child replies 'even' or 'odd' and names the units digit. A brisk, playful finish that consolidates the digit-based rule.

periods.teacher_notes: Children may initially think there are more even numbers because even numbers 'feel bigger' or because the series starts with 2 and ends with 100; the counting activity itself resolves this. The digit-based quick-fire round at the close draws together the pairing model from the even-and-odd unit, the chart pattern from the crayons arrangement unit, and the consecutive-number generalisation — making the connections explicit without re-teaching any of them.
materials: Textbook open to p.37 (crayons chart) and p.38

items.prompt: Mango trees are planted in 4 rows. Each row has 6 trees. Draw rings around equal groups of trees and write the total number of trees.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 24 trees. The child should show 4 groups of 6 (or 6 groups of 4) circled and write 24.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Group the trees into equal rows and count all the groups together.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the child draw dots for each tree and circle rows; stretch: ask how the count changes if one more row is added.

exercise.description: Count the coconut trees in Gundappa's land from the top-view grid. Write the number. How do you know?

items.prompt: Raju arranges his coins in a circle: four ₹5 coins and three ₹2 coins. How much money is in the circle?

teacher_guide.method_one_line: Multiply each denomination by its count and add the two totals.

what_each_option_reveals.B: Child counted only the ₹5 coins and ignored the ₹2 coins.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Child counted only the ₹2 coins and ignored the ₹5 coins.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Child added the number of coins (7) to the face value of one denomination, or confused count with value.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the child pick out play coins and physically count each group; stretch: ask what different coin combination also makes ₹26.

exercise.description: Look at Shirley's coin arrangement (circular pattern). How much money is it?

items.prompt: Use play money (₹1, ₹2, ₹5, ₹10 coins and notes) to show the amount ₹47. Draw or list the coins and notes you chose. Is there another way to make ₹47?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Any valid combination totalling ₹47, for example four ₹10 notes and one ₹5 coin and two ₹1 coins. A second valid combination is also acceptable.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Select the highest denomination that fits, subtract, then repeat for the remainder.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: start the child with a ₹10 note and ask how much more is needed; stretch: challenge the child to find the combination using the fewest coins and notes.

exercise.description: Arrange play money of amounts 1, 2, 5, and 10 to show ₹36, ₹125, and ₹183. Ask your peers to tell how much it is.

items.prompt: Look at the page numbers 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 in any book. Draw a square around each even page number and a circle around each odd page number. What pattern do you see?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Squares on 2, 4, 6 and circles on 1, 3, 5. The pattern is: odd, even, odd, even — they alternate.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Check whether each number pairs completely into twos; those that do are even, those with one left over are odd.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the child pair counters under each number before marking; stretch: ask whether the alternating pattern continues past 6 and how they know.

exercise.description: Explore your textbook and find out what Shirley has seen. Draw a square on the even page numbers. Put a circle on the odd page numbers.

items.prompt: Priya counts a pile of ₹5 coins by grouping them in threes. Suresh counts the same pile by grouping them in fives. Priya says she counted 4 groups; Suresh says he counted groups too. Will they get the same total? How did each of them count? Explain.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Yes, both get the same total because the pile has not changed. Priya skip-counts in groups of 3 coins (each ₹5), Suresh in groups of 5 coins (each ₹5). The grouping strategy differs but the total is the same.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Recognise that different groupings of the same set always produce the same total count.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: ask the child to act it out with counters in two different groupings; stretch: ask which grouping is quicker and why.

exercise.description: How did you count them? Discuss in class.

items.prompt: Rani arranges 12 coins in groups of 4 and writes the total in a triangle. Dev arranges the same 12 coins in groups of 3. Draw both arrangements in your own way and fill in the triangle for each. Are the totals the same?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Both totals are 12 coins. Rani has 3 groups of 4; Dev has 4 groups of 3. The totals are the same because the number of coins did not change.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Arrange equal groups and count all groups to find the total; different groupings of the same set give the same total.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: provide coins or counters to physically build both arrangements; stretch: ask the child to find a third way to arrange 12 coins in equal groups.

exercise.description: Shirley and Shiv arranged coins in groups. Write the number of coins in the blank triangles for each arrangement.

items.prompt: Arun lists the first eight numbers in the times-2 table: 2, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12, 14, 16. He pairs each number into twos. What does he notice?

options.label: A
options.text: Every number has one left over, so they are all odd.

options.label: B
options.text: Every number pairs perfectly with no one left over, so they are all even.

options.label: C
options.text: Only the larger numbers pair perfectly; the smaller ones do not.

options.label: D
options.text: Some pair perfectly and some have one left over, so half are even and half are odd.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Every number pairs perfectly with none left over, so all numbers in the times-2 table are even.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Pair each multiple of 2 into twos and check whether any are left over.

what_each_option_reveals.A: Child applied the odd-number rule (one left over) without testing — likely confused 'times-2' with an odd pattern.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Child has not yet generalised the pairing result and is guessing based on appearance of large vs small numbers.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Child incorrectly believes the pairing rule depends on the size of the number rather than the pairing outcome.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: have the child physically pair counters for 2, 4, and 6 before answering; stretch: ask whether any multiple of 2 could ever be odd and how they know.

exercise.description: Do you think all numbers in the times-2 table are even?

items.prompt: Pick any odd number between 10 and 20. Write the number that comes just before it and the number that comes just after it. Are those neighbours even or odd? Now do the same for any even number between 10 and 20. What do you notice?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: The numbers before and after an odd number are always even; the numbers before and after an even number are always odd. The child should notice the alternating pattern in both cases.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Check the units digit of each neighbour to classify it, then state the alternating rule.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: use the crayons chart (p.37) to locate the number and look left and right; stretch: ask whether this holds for numbers beyond 20 and how they are sure.

exercise.description: Shirley notices numbers before and after an odd number are even. Shiv wonders if numbers before and after an even number are odd. Check and discuss.

items.prompt: Which of the following numbers is even? Explain by looking at its last digit.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 300 is even because its units digit is 0, which pairs completely with no remainder.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Look only at the units digit; if it is 0, 2, 4, 6, or 8, the number is even.

what_each_option_reveals.D: Child looked at the hundreds digit (4) instead of the units digit (5), choosing 415 because 4 is even.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Child may have thought 9 and 9 together make an even pattern, or confused the repeated digit for an even number.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Child may have confused a familiar small odd number for an even one, or checked no digit at all.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: write only the units digit of each option and have the child classify that single digit; stretch: ask the child to make a four-digit even number and explain their choice of last digit.

exercise.description: Identify which of the following numbers are even and which are odd. Explain your reasoning: 30, 78, 300, 415, 46, 67, 154, 99.

items.prompt: Count all even numbers from 1 to 10 and all odd numbers from 1 to 10. Write them in two lists. Are there more even or more odd numbers, or are the counts equal? Use this to explain what you would expect between 1 and 100.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Even numbers 1–10: 2, 4, 6, 8, 10 — five in all. Odd numbers 1–10: 1, 3, 5, 7, 9 — five in all. The counts are equal. Between 1 and 100 the counts are also equal (50 even, 50 odd) because the alternating pattern continues throughout.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: List and count each group; apply the alternating pattern to generalise.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: provide a printed 1–10 number strip and have the child colour even and odd in different colours; stretch: ask whether the counts remain equal between 1 and 101 and why.

exercise.description: Are there more even or odd numbers between 1 and 100?

items.prompt: Which number from the list below is odd?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 17 is odd because when its counters are paired in twos, one is left over (units digit 7 is odd).
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Check the units digit — 7 leaves a remainder of 1 when divided into pairs of 2.

what_each_option_reveals.A: Child may have chosen a number ending in 4 thinking 'not a round number means odd'.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Child is not yet applying the pairing rule and is guessing.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Child chose 20, likely unfamiliar with the pairing test and guessing from position in the list.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: have the child draw 17 dots and pair them to find the leftover; stretch: ask the child to name the next three odd numbers after 17.

exercise.description: Identify numbers between 1 and 20 as even or odd. You may draw the pairing arrangement.

items.prompt: A child circles all odd numbers and squares all even numbers from this set: 9, 24, 51, 38. Which list shows the odd numbers correctly?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 9 and 51 are odd (units digits 9 and 1); 24 and 38 are even (units digits 4 and 8).
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Check the units digit of each number against the even-digit set (0, 2, 4, 6, 8); any other units digit is odd.

what_each_option_reveals.C: Child reversed the classification — selected the even numbers as odd.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Child correctly identified 9 as odd but misclassified 38 (even) as odd, likely distracted by the 3 in the tens place.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Child correctly identified 51 as odd but misclassified 24 (even) as odd, likely distracted by the 2 in the tens place.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: write only the units digit of each number and classify that digit alone; stretch: ask the child to add one more odd number to the set and justify the choice.

exercise.description: Circle the odd numbers and put a square around each even number from the given set (5, 8, 36, 69, 22, 51, 30, 38, 37, 52, 43). Use the crayons arrangement if needed.

items.prompt: Orange trees are planted in 6 rows with 4 trees in each row. A farmer picks 3 oranges from every tree. How many oranges does the farmer pick in all?

teacher_guide.method_one_line: First count total trees by grouping rows, then multiply by the number of oranges per tree.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: draw the 6-row array first, count trees by circling rows, then skip-count in threes; stretch: ask how many oranges if 2 more rows were added.
